hints: Think why every NMR spectrum needs a fixed zero point that is inert, soluble and gives one sharp singlet away from other signals.
walkthrough:
Fix the zero with TMS**
Think of TMS, $\text{Si}(\text{CH}_{3})_{4}$, as your ruler zero. It is inert, soluble in organic solvents, volatile so easily removed, and has 12 equivalent protons in a highly shielded environment. That gives one intense singlet set exactly at $\delta = 0$, well away from almost all organic protons.

Use D2O to find exchangeable protons**
Now picture $\text{O-H}$ and $\text{N-H}$ protons. They are labile and exchange with deuterium: $\text{R-O-H} + \text{D}_{2}\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{R-O-D} + \text{HOD}$. Deuterium does not show in $^{1}\text{H}$ NMR, so any $\text{O-H}$ or $\text{N-H}$ peak disappears after shaking with $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$. That disappearance identifies the labile proton.

Final answer: TMS: reference standard to define $\delta = 0$.
$\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$: solvent for exchange to identify $\text{O-H}$ / $\text{N-H}$ protons, peaks disappear on shaking with $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$.

hints: Draw each ketone fully and label every $\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{CH}_{2}$ and $\text{CH}$ group, then look for a plane of symmetry that makes groups equivalent.
Remember each set of equivalent protons gives one $^{1}\text{H}$ peak and each set of equivalent carbons gives one $^{13}\text{C}$ peak, including the $\text{C=O}$ carbon.
walkthrough:
Count proton environments in pentan-2-one**
Draw $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. No symmetry here. The left $\text{CH}_{3}$ next to $\text{C=O}$, the $\text{CH}_{2}$ next to $\text{C=O}$, the middle $\text{CH}_{2}$ and the end $\text{CH}_{3}$ are all in different environments. That is 4 proton peaks. All 5 carbons are different, so 5 carbon-13 peaks.

Use symmetry in pentan-3-one**
Draw $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. This molecule is symmetrical about the $\text{C=O}$. The two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups are equivalent to each other and the two $\text{CH}_{2}$ groups are equivalent to each other. That gives only 2 proton peaks. For carbon, two $\text{CH}_{3}$ as one, two $\text{CH}_{2}$ as one, plus $\text{C=O}$ as one, total 3 carbon-13 peaks.

Spot the equivalent methyls in 3-methylbutanone**
Draw $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}$. The two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups on the $\text{CH}$ end are equivalent. So you have: $\text{CH}_{3}$ next to $\text{C=O}$ as one, $\text{CH}$ as one, and $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}$ as one, total 3 proton peaks. For carbon: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C=O}$ as one, $\text{C=O}$ as one, $\text{CH}$ as one, $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}$ as one, total 4 carbon-13 peaks.

hints: Recall the n+1 rule: a proton with n equivalent protons on adjacent carbons is split into n+1 peaks.
Look for a $\text{CH}_{3}$ next to a $\text{CH}$ to give a doublet, and a $\text{CH}_{3}$ next to a carbon with no protons, such as $\text{C=O}$, to give a singlet.
walkthrough:
Find where a doublet must come from**
A doublet means n = 1, so the protons have exactly one neighbouring proton. Only 3-methylbutanone, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}$, has $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}$ next to one $\text{CH}$ proton. Those six equivalent methyl protons are split by the one $\text{CH}$ into a doublet. Neither pentan-2-one nor pentan-3-one has a $\text{CH}_{3}$ next to a $\text{CH}$.

Find where a singlet must come from**
A singlet means n = 0, so no protons on the adjacent carbon. Both pentan-2-one ($\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}-$) and 3-methylbutanone ($\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}-$) have a methyl directly attached to $\text{C=O}$, whose carbon bears no protons, so that $\text{CH}_{3}$ appears as a singlet. Pentan-3-one has only $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}-$, so its $\text{CH}_{3}$ is split by $\text{CH}_{2}$ into a triplet, not a singlet.

Final answer: a doublet: 3-methylbutanone only.
a singlet: pentan-2-one and 3-methylbutanone.

hints: Apply the strict test for a chiral carbon: a tetrahedral carbon attached to four different atoms or groups, so exclude any $\text{C=O}$, $\text{C=C}$ or $\text{CH}_{2}$ or $\text{CH}_{3}$ or $\text{C}(\text{OH})$ with two identical ring paths.
walkthrough:
Apply the four different groups test**
Go round the cortisone skeleton in Fig. 7.1 and cross out every carbon that cannot be chiral. All $\text{C=O}$ carbons are planar, the $\text{C=C}$ carbons are planar, all $\text{CH}_{2}$ carbons have two H atoms, and all $\text{CH}_{3}$ carbons have three H atoms. Only tetrahedral $\text{CH}$ or C carbons at ring junctions and substituted centres can qualify.

Count the survivors**
Checking each ring junction $\text{CH}$ and the substituted quaternary carbons, six carbons each carry four different chains, including the ring fusion points and the $\text{C-OH}$ bearing carbon on the five membered ring. That gives 6 chiral centres in one molecule.

hints: Recall that excess $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols but does not reduce isolated or conjugated $\text{C=C}$ under these conditions, so count how many $\text{C=O}$ ketone groups are present in cortisone.
walkthrough:
Count reducible carbonyls**
Look at Fig. 7.1. Cortisone, $\text{C}_{21}\text{H}_{28}\text{O}_{5}$, contains three ketone $\text{C=O}$ groups and one $\text{C=C}$ bond. $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ in excess will reduce each ketone to a secondary or tertiary alcohol: $\text{R}_{2}\text{C=O} + 2[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{R}_{2}\text{CH-OH}$, but it leaves the $\text{C=C}$ untouched.

Add the hydrogens**
Each $\text{C=O}$ to $\text{CH-OH}$ adds 2 H atoms with O unchanged. For three ketones: $28 + (3 \times 2) = 34$ H. Carbon and oxygen numbers are unchanged. So the product is $\text{C}_{21}\text{H}_{34}\text{O}_{5}$.

hints: Think what happens when plane-polarised light passes through a solution of a single chiral molecule compared with an achiral solution.
walkthrough:
Picture rotating light**
Imagine plane-polarised light as a wave vibrating in one plane only. When it passes through a solution containing a chiral, non-racemic molecule like cortisone, the interaction with the asymmetric electron distribution twists that plane by a measurable angle. That ability to rotate the plane of polarised light is exactly what optically active means.
Final answer: A substance able to rotate the plane of polarised light.
